analysis.one_liner: Guarantees full Social Security payments if trust funds run dry and fast-tracks taxing the rich to fix it.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote or any committee action in the House and died when the 118th Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would guarantee that Social Security keeps paying full benefits even if its trust funds run short, by automatically sending the program whatever money it needs each month. It would also require a Social Security field office in every county with more than 150,000 people, and it would create a special fast-track procedure: if a trust fund ever became insolvent, a bill to fix it would be forced to the floor in both chambers within days, with no amendments allowed, limited debate, and its contents pre-set by the bill itself — no benefit cuts, and any new money raised only from the ultra-wealthy and corporations. The bill was introduced in August 2024, never got a committee vote, and expired at the end of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries and their families. The bill's own findings note that nearly 9 out of 10 people age 65 and older receive benefits, more than 9 million veterans get Social Security, and over 6 million children depend on it [S2]. The automatic funding guarantee would protect those checks if the trust funds ran dry, and the field office requirement would help beneficiaries — especially older or disabled people who cannot get help online or by phone — reach in-person service [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and their families

how_it_helps.text: Once the Commissioner of Social Security certifies that either trust fund cannot pay benefits, the bill automatically appropriates, monthly, whatever amount is needed for the Social Security Administration to keep paying benefits — so checks would not stop or shrink while Congress argued [S2].
It requires a field office in every county with more than 150,000 residents, addressing access for people who cannot seek help online or over the phone [S2].

If a trust fund becomes insolvent, a solvency bill would bypass normal committee delays and Senate filibuster practice: committees would have 5 days to report or be discharged, debate would be capped (10 hours in the Senate), no amendments would be allowed, and a final vote would come within days [S2].
The fast-track bill's contents are fixed in advance: full benefits continue, no benefit cuts, and any additional needed funds 'borne by the ultra-wealthy and corporations' [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If the automatic funding guarantee and the fast-track solvency mechanism ever activated, the cost would fall on very high-income households and corporations, since the bill specifies that any additional needed funds must be borne by the ultra-wealthy and corporations [S2]. Taxpayers generally would also backstop the automatic monthly appropriations in the meantime.

drawbacks.text: Section 4 writes a blank check: it appropriates monthly whatever amount the trust funds need, with no dedicated revenue source and no limit, and that guarantee operates indefinitely while the solvency fix only kicks in after insolvency is certified [S2].

The fast-track procedure bars every amendment in both chambers, caps Senate debate at 10 hours, and waives normal points of order — overriding the Senate's usual extended-debate rules and concentrating decisions in the two party leaders' hands [S2].
The field office mandate has no funding attached, creating an unfunded operating requirement for the Social Security Administration [S2].

Section 5 pre-decides the content of any future solvency bill — no benefit cuts, taxes only on the wealthy and corporations — before a crisis arrives, removing the ability of future Congresses to weigh other approaches such as gradual revenue adjustments or administrative reforms [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise — benefits never stop while Congress dithers — is genuinely protective for tens of millions of households, and fast-tracking a fix once insolvency hits is a real response to a real deadline. But the bill is a blunt instrument: an unlimited automatic appropriation, a solvency bill whose content is written in advance, and a no-amendments fast-track that trades deliberation for speed. The field office requirement is sensible on its face but unfunded. It reads as both a safety guarantee and a statement of priorities, and its procedural design would be contested on its merits even by people who support protecting benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees, later to the Social Security subcommittee, and sat there until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 — no markup, no vote, no floor action ever took place.

narrative.text: Rep. Pat Ryan introduced the bill on August 9, 2024, less than three months before the election [S1][S4].
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, for relevant provisions, the Rules Committee [S4].
On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security — the only action after introduction — and it never advanced further before the Congress ended [S4].

The bill's findings explicitly frame it against named Republican leaders — former President Trump, Speaker Mike Johnson, J.D. Vance, and Rick Scott — and cite a House Republican Study Committee plan that would raise the retirement age to 69 [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No benefits changed hands either way, since the bill's funding guarantee never took effect. The practical beneficiaries of its failure are very high-income households and corporations, who are spared the pre-set fast-track to new taxes the bill would have created had a trust fund ever been certified insolvent, along with whoever preferred not to have that debate forced to the floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households and corporations spared its tax pathway

for.name: Rep. Patrick Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 9, 2024, combining a benefits guarantee, a field office mandate, and a fast-track solvency procedure with tax increases limited to the ultra-wealthy and corporations.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction (Chair Jason Smith, R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill, held no markup, and referred it to the Social Security subcommittee on December 17, 2024, where it remained until the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for House floor consideration at any point in the five months it was pending.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll call; the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat, it drew zero cosponsors, and its findings name four Republican leaders as threats to Social Security [S2][S3].

industries.note: Had the bill's fast-track ever activated, any solvency fix would by law have to be funded by them, since the bill requires additional funds to be 'borne by the ultra-wealthy and corporations' [S2]. Their interest in avoiding that tax exposure runs against beneficiaries' interest in uninterrupted benefits.
The bill would give the agency guaranteed monthly appropriations to keep paying benefits during any shortfall and mandate a field office network reaching every county over 150,000 people [S2].
